section.title: The Tabernacle
section.sectionRationale: Having described the furnishings that will fill it, God now gives Moses the pattern for the tabernacle structure itself: its linen and goat hair coverings, its acacia wood frames, and the veil that will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.
section.thesis: God instructs Moses to build the tabernacle in layers, from its inner curtains of linen and cherubim to its outer coverings and standing frames, and to hang a veil that separates the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place where the ark rests.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the inner linen curtains woven with cherubim; the outer coverings of goat hair, ram skins, and fine leather; the acacia wood frames that give the tent its shape; and the veil that divides the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.

media.alt: Linen curtains joined with gold clasps
media.caption: Ten curtains of linen and blue, purple, and scarlet yarn are joined into a single tabernacle.

verses.text: “You are to construct the {{tabernacle|tabernacle}} itself with ten curtains of finely spun linen, each with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and cherubim skillfully worked into them.
Each curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide, all curtains the same size.
Five of the curtains are to be joined together, and the other five joined as well.
Make loops of blue material on the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and do the same for the end curtain in the second set.
Make fifty loops on one curtain and fifty loops on the end curtain of the second set, so that the loops line up opposite one another.
Make fifty gold clasps as well, and join the curtains together with the clasps, so that the tabernacle will be a unit.

units.label: The outer coverings
units.note: goat hair, ram skins, fine leather

verses.text: You are to make curtains of goat hair for the tent over the tabernacle, eleven curtains in all.
Each of the eleven curtains is to be the same size, thirty cubits long and four cubits wide.
Join five of the curtains into one set and the other six into another. Then fold the sixth curtain over double at the front of the tent.
Make fifty loops along the edge of the end curtain in the first set, and fifty loops along the edge of the corresponding curtain in the second set.
Make fifty bronze clasps and put them through the loops to join the tent together as a unit.
As for the overlap that remains of the tent curtains, the half curtain that is left over shall hang down over the back of the tabernacle.
And the tent curtains will be a cubit longer on either side, and the excess will hang over the sides of the tabernacle to cover it.
Also make a covering for the tent out of ram skins dyed red, and over that a covering of fine leather.

units.label: The upright frames
units.note: according to the pattern shown you on the mountain

verses.text: You are to construct upright frames of acacia wood for the tabernacle.
Each frame is to be ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide.
Two tenons must be connected to each other for each frame. Make all the frames of the tabernacle in this way.
Construct twenty frames for the south side of the tabernacle,
with forty silver bases under the twenty frames, two bases for each frame, one under each tenon.
For the second side of the tabernacle, the north side, make twenty frames
and forty silver bases, two bases under each frame.
Make six frames for the rear of the tabernacle, the west side,
and two frames for the two back corners of the tabernacle,
coupled together from bottom to top and fitted into a single ring. These will serve as the two corners.
So there are to be eight frames and sixteen silver bases, two under each frame.
You are also to make five crossbars of acacia wood for the frames on one side of the tabernacle,
five for those on the other side, and five for those on the rear side of the tabernacle, to the west.
The central crossbar in the middle of the frames shall extend from one end to the other.
Overlay the frames with gold and make gold rings to hold the crossbars. Also overlay the crossbars with gold.
So you are to set up the tabernacle according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.

units.label: The veil and the screen
units.note: separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place

media.alt: A woven veil hung on gold hooks before a hidden ark
media.caption: The veil shields the ark of the Testimony behind it, separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.

verses.text: Make a {{veil|veil}} of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it.
Hang it with gold hooks on four posts of acacia wood, overlaid with gold and standing on four silver bases.
And hang the veil from the clasps and place the ark of the Testimony behind the veil. So the veil will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.
Put the mercy seat on the ark of the Testimony in the Most Holy Place.
And place the table outside the veil on the north side of the tabernacle, and put the lampstand opposite the table, on the south side.
For the entrance to the tent, you are to make a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen.
Make five posts of acacia wood for the curtain, overlay them with gold hooks, and cast five bronze bases for them.

tabernacle.gloss: Dwelling place, from the same root as the verb to dwell. The tabernacle is literally God's tent, a portable dwelling that travels with Israel through the wilderness, always among His people rather than fixed in one distant place.

veil.gloss: The inner veil, a heavy woven curtain separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place where the ark rested. It marked how restricted access to God's immediate presence was under the old covenant, entered only once a year by the high priest.

basic.context: After describing the furnishings, God now gives the pattern for the tabernacle itself: layers of curtains, a wooden frame structure, and a veil separating the Holy Place from the innermost Most Holy Place where the ark sat. Every layer moves from the most costly and beautiful materials closest to God's presence toward plainer materials on the outside.
basic.hermeneutics: These are literal, practical building instructions for Israel's actual portable sanctuary, not primarily a code to decode. The structure itself communicates something true without needing every measurement to carry separate symbolism: increasing holiness the closer one moves toward the ark, and real, careful separation between a holy God and sinful people.
basic.originalLanguages: The mishkan, dwelling place, is God's tent, moving with His people rather than remaining fixed. The parokhet, veil, woven with cherubim like the ones guarding Eden, keeps the way to the Most Holy Place shut, a visible, physical reminder that access to God's presence remains restricted under this covenant.
basic.typology: The veil separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place points forward to the barrier sin creates between people and God, a barrier torn in two at the moment of Christ's death, Matthew 27:51. The tabernacle itself, God's dwelling among His people, anticipates the incarnation, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
basic.christ: John says the Word became flesh and 'tabernacled' among us, John 1:14, using the very language of this structure to describe Jesus. When Jesus died, the temple veil was torn from top to bottom, showing that the separation this tabernacle maintained has been decisively ended in Him, Hebrews 10:19-20.
basic.god: God's holiness required careful, deliberate separation, layer after layer, from ordinary people, yet His whole purpose was still to dwell among them. Even in the most restrictive structure, His desire for nearness to His people is unmistakable.
basic.crossReferences: John 1:14 says the Word tabernacled among us. Matthew 27:51 records the temple veil torn in two at Christ's death. Hebrews 9:1-8 explains the two chambers and their meaning. Hebrews 10:19-20 says believers now have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place through Christ's flesh.
basic.oneStory: God gives detailed instructions for a dwelling that keeps His holy presence carefully separated from sinful people by curtain after curtain and a final veil. That separation is exactly what Christ ends: He tabernacles among us in the flesh, and His death tears the veil, opening the way into God's presence forever.

context.literary:
Exodus 26 moves in a loop. It begins with the innermost layer, the linen curtains that form the tabernacle proper, verses 1 to 6. It then works outward through the goat hair tent and the two coverings of skin, verses 7 to 14. It turns to the frames that hold everything up, verses 15 to 30. And then it comes back inside to hang the veil and to place the ark, the table and the lampstand, verses 31 to 35, before closing with the screen at the entrance, verses 36 and 37. The chapter ties itself to chapter 25 by returning at the end to the furnishings already described.

Two refrains organise the material. The first is that the parts are to be joined 'so that the tabernacle will be a unit,' verse 6, and 'to join the tent together as a unit,' verse 11. Many pieces make one dwelling. The second is the reminder of verse 30, 'according to the pattern shown you on the mountain,' which echoes Exodus 25:9 and 25:40 and will return in 27:8.

The materials are graded by nearness. Gold clasps join the inner curtains, verse 6; bronze clasps join the goat hair tent, verse 11. The frames are overlaid with gold and stand on silver bases, verses 19 and 29. The veil and the entrance screen use the same fine yarns, but only the veil has cherubim worked into it, verses 31 and 36. The closer one comes to the ark, the more precious the material and the more heavenly the decoration.

The dimensions also carry a quiet design. Twenty frames a cubit and a half wide give a length of thirty cubits; each frame is ten cubits high. The veil hangs from the clasps, verse 33, which many readers place twenty cubits from the entrance. If so, the Most Holy Place formed a cube of ten cubits, anticipating the cube of Solomon's inner sanctuary, 1 Kings 6:20, and the cube of the New Jerusalem, Revelation 21:16.
context.historical:
The tabernacle was a portable sanctuary for a people on the move, and Exodus 26 reads like the design for a tent that can be taken apart and rebuilt many times. Numbers 4 assigns the work of carrying it. The Gershonites carried the curtains and coverings, Numbers 4:25-26, and the Merarites the frames, crossbars, posts and bases, Numbers 4:31-32. The clasps, loops, tenons and rings described so carefully here are what made that possible.

The coverings would have been familiar to people who lived in tents. Goat hair was, and still is, a common material for tents in the region because it sheds rain. Ram skins dyed red and a covering of fine leather went over it. The BSB footnote notes that the last may have been the hides of large aquatic mammals, which would have made a tough, weatherproof outer layer. From outside the tabernacle looked plain. Its glory was on the inside.

The blue, purple and scarlet yarns were costly dyes in the ancient world, and purple especially was associated with kings, Judges 8:26 and Esther 8:15. The inner curtains and the veil were a royal textile. The fine linen was a product Egypt was known for, which fits a people who had lived there and left with Egyptian goods.

The silver bases have a striking origin. Exodus 30:11-16 required every counted man to pay half a shekel as 'a ransom for his life,' and Exodus 38:25-27 records that this silver was used to cast the bases of the sanctuary and the veil, a hundred bases in all. The forty bases on each side, sixteen at the rear and four under the veil posts make exactly that number. The whole house of God stood on the atonement money of His people.

The tabernacle later stood at Shiloh, Joshua 18:1, and in David's time at Gibeon, 1 Chronicles 21:29, until the temple replaced it.
context.canonical:
The tent remains in Israel's memory long after it is folded away. When David proposes a house of cedar, God answers, 'I have moved about with a tent as My dwelling,' 2 Samuel 7:6, as if He preferred to travel with His people. The psalmists turn the tent into a picture of safety: 'O LORD, who may abide in Your tent?' Psalm 15:1, and 'He will conceal me under the cover of His tent,' Psalm 27:5. Isaiah calls restored Zion to 'enlarge the site of your tent,' Isaiah 54:2, and Amos promises to 'restore the fallen tent of David,' Amos 9:11, a promise James applies to the gathering of the Gentiles, Acts 15:16.

The veil passed into the temple, where Solomon made one 'of blue, purple, and crimson yarn and fine linen, with cherubim woven into it,' 2 Chronicles 3:14. All three Synoptic Gospels record that the temple veil was torn at the death of Jesus, Matthew 27:51, Mark 15:38 and Luke 23:45, and Matthew and Mark say it was 'torn in two from top to bottom.'

Hebrews builds much of its argument on this chapter. It describes the two rooms, Hebrews 9:2-3, and says that as long as the first tabernacle stood 'the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed,' Hebrews 9:8. Christ has passed through 'the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands,' Hebrews 9:11, and believers enter 'through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:20. Hope itself is an anchor that 'enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain,' Hebrews 6:19.

John says the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. Paul and Peter call the human body a tent, 2 Corinthians 5:1-4 and 2 Peter 1:13-14. Revelation sees 'the tabernacle of the Testimony' opened in heaven, Revelation 15:5, and promises that God 'will spread His tabernacle over them,' Revelation 7:15.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wants Israel to understand that the God who met them on the mountain would now go with them. The loops, clasps, rings and bases show a dwelling designed to be dismantled, carried and set up again. The God of Sinai is not tied to a mountain.

He also wants them to see how holiness is ordered. The layers of the tent, the grading of materials and the veil all say that God's presence is at the centre of the camp and yet cannot be approached casually. The ark is placed 'behind the veil,' verse 33, and the veil 'will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.' Israel was to live with a God who is near and a God who is holy, and to learn to hold both.

The cherubim woven into the curtains and the veil would have reminded Israel of Eden, where cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life, Genesis 3:24. The message is double. The dwelling is a way back toward God's presence, yet the way is still guarded.

Finally, the repeated call to make everything 'according to the pattern,' verse 30, teaches that the way to God is His to design. Israel's part was faithful obedience in every detail, which the closing chapters of Exodus record, Exodus 40:16.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The instructions were prescriptive for Israel in the wilderness and were carried out, Exodus 36:8-38. They are not prescriptions for church buildings. The New Testament never asks Christians to reproduce the tabernacle, and it treats the structure as a shadow of heavenly realities, Hebrews 8:5 and 9:24.

Two kinds of error are possible. One treats the chapter as irrelevant because its rules have expired. The other turns it into an allegory where every clasp and bar has a hidden spiritual meaning. The better path listens to what the New Testament itself draws from it: the veil and the two rooms, Hebrews 9:8, and the idea of God dwelling in a tent, John 1:14.

What does carry forward is the theology. God still desires to dwell with His people, now by His Spirit in the church, Ephesians 2:21-22. Access to Him is still His gift, now opened through Christ, Hebrews 10:19-20. And the careful, skilled work of the craftsmen who wove the curtains still shows that making things well for God's glory is a form of worship.

debates.question: How literally should later interpreters press the exact measurements and materials of the tabernacle for theological meaning?

views.label: Focus on the broad structure
views.case: Many interpreters caution against extracting symbolic meaning from every measurement or clasp. Scripture explains only some elements, such as the veil's function, and does not gloss most of the numbers. Pressing the details can produce readings that owe more to the reader's imagination than to the text.

views.label: Attention to what Scripture itself highlights
views.case: Others note that Hebrews 9 draws real theological weight from the two chamber structure and the veil, and that the grading of materials and the cherubim clearly carry meaning. The major features, though not every measurement, are intended to teach.

debates.bearing: Both approaches affirm the central point: a graded structure kept sinful people at a distance from God's presence, and that distance is what Christ has closed. Details should be pressed only as far as Scripture presses them.

debates.question: Were the qerashim of verses 15 to 29 solid boards or open frames?

views.label: Solid boards
views.case: Older English versions, following a long tradition, render the word 'boards,' picturing solid planks of acacia laid edge to edge to form walls. On this view the Holy Place was fully enclosed by gold covered walls.

views.label: Open frames
views.case: Many modern translators, including the BSB, prefer 'frames.' Solid planks ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide would be very heavy for a portable structure, and each piece has two tenons, verse 17, which suits a frame of two uprights joined by crossbars. On this view the embroidered linen with its cherubim would have been visible from inside between the uprights.

debates.bearing: The question is about construction, not doctrine, and certainty is not possible. The frame reading has the advantage of letting the cherubim curtains, which the text lavishes attention on, be seen from within, which suits the chapter's emphasis on the beauty of the inner dwelling.

debates.question: What does the tearing of the temple veil at Jesus' death signify?

views.label: The way into God's presence opened
views.case: Hebrews 10:19-20 speaks of 'the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body.' On this reading the torn veil means that access to the Most Holy Place, once restricted to the high priest once a year, Hebrews 9:7, is now open to all who come through Christ.

views.label: Judgment on the temple
views.case: Jesus had predicted that not one stone of the temple would be left on another, Matthew 24:2. The tearing of the veil from top to bottom can be read as God's own act ending the temple's role, a sign that its sacrifices were finished.

views.label: God coming out to the world
views.case: Mark uses the same verb for the heavens 'breaking open' at Jesus' baptism, Mark 1:10, and for the veil, Mark 15:38. On this view God's presence is breaking out from behind the curtain, and the next words in Mark are a Gentile centurion confessing the Son of God.

debates.bearing: These are not rivals. The tearing is from top to bottom, God's act, and it both ends the old order and opens a new way. The veil no longer marks where sinners must stop but where Christ has gone before them, Hebrews 6:19-20.

study.originalLanguages:
Exodus 26 keeps two words for the structure carefully apart. The linen curtains of verse 1 form the mishkan, 'the tabernacle itself.' The goat hair curtains of verse 7 form 'the tent over the tabernacle,' and the word for tent is ohel. The mishkan is the dwelling, the inner house of God; the ohel is the covering that shelters it. The phrase 'Tent of Meeting,' ohel mo'ed, uses the second word and names the tent by what happens in it, meeting.

Verse 6 says the curtains are joined 'so that the tabernacle will be a unit,' and verse 11 says the same of the tent. The Hebrew is simply echad, 'one.' The chapter describes dozens of separate pieces, but its goal is a single dwelling.

The cherubim in verses 1 and 31 are 'skillfully worked,' ma'aseh choshev, literally 'the work of a designer.' The root chashav means to think, plan or devise. It is the verb used of Bezalel, filled with the Spirit 'to design artistic works,' Exodus 35:32. The Spirit of God is associated here with artistic imagination as well as with prophecy and leadership.

The three colours of verse 1 are tekhelet, blue, argaman, purple, and tola'at shani, scarlet, the last literally 'worm of scarlet,' because the dye came from an insect. Tekhelet is the colour of the cord Israelites were to wear on their tassels, Numbers 15:38. The same colours appear in the high priest's garments in Exodus 28.

The veil of verse 31 is parokhet, the word Scripture regularly uses for this inner curtain, and it is carefully distinguished from the screen at the entrance in verse 36, masakh. The noun masakh comes from a verb meaning to screen or cover, the same verb used when the cherubim are 'overshadowing the mercy seat,' Exodus 25:20. The entrance screen covers the way in; the cherubim cover the place of meeting.

The two rooms in verse 33 are 'the Holy Place,' haqqodesh, and 'the Most Holy Place,' qodesh haqqodashim, literally 'the holy of the holies,' as the BSB footnote notes. Hebrew forms a superlative by this kind of doubling, as in 'song of songs.' It is the most holy place there is.

The Greek translators used skene, 'tent,' for this structure, and the veil is katapetasma, the word the Gospels use when 'the veil of the temple was torn,' Mark 15:38, and that Hebrews uses of 'the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:20. John's statement that the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, uses a verb built on skene. Revelation 21:3 uses the same family of words: 'the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.'

typology.type: The tabernacle, God's tent among His people, Exodus 26:1-30
typology.fulfillment: God lived in a tent in the middle of Israel's camp, hidden behind curtains and skins. John says the eternal Word 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, with a verb that means to pitch a tent. Jesus also speaks of His body as the temple, John 2:19-21. The escalation is that God no longer lives near His people in a structure of cloth and wood but has taken their own flesh. The type falls short because the tabernacle concealed God's glory, while in Christ 'we have seen His glory,' full of grace and truth.

typology.type: The veil before the Most Holy Place, Exodus 26:31-33
typology.fulfillment: The veil, woven with cherubim, blocked the way to the ark, and only the high priest could pass it, once a year and never without blood, Hebrews 9:7. Hebrews says believers enter 'by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:20, linking the veil with Christ's flesh given in death. At that death the temple veil was torn from top to bottom, Mark 15:38. The type is reversed in its fulfilment: what once kept people out becomes, in Christ, the very way in.

typology.type: The earthly tent made by hands, Exodus 26:30
typology.fulfillment: The tabernacle was built to a pattern shown on the mountain, and Hebrews reads it as a copy of a heavenly reality. Christ 'went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands,' Hebrews 9:11, and ministers 'in the sanctuary and true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man,' Hebrews 8:2. The escalation is from copy to original, from a tent Aaron entered once a year to heaven itself, where Christ appears for us, Hebrews 9:24. The earthly type could be folded, carried and eventually lost; the true tabernacle cannot.

typology.type: The portable tent of a pilgrim people, Exodus 26:6 and 26:15-30
typology.fulfillment: The tabernacle was designed to be taken down and carried until Israel reached the land. The patriarchs 'lived in tents' as they looked for a city 'whose architect and builder is God,' Hebrews 11:9-10. Paul calls the present body 'the earthly tent we live in,' longing for 'an eternal house in heaven,' 2 Corinthians 5:1. The church, too, is being built together into God's dwelling, Ephesians 2:22, while still on the road. The type points to rest: in the end God 'will spread His tabernacle over them,' Revelation 7:15, and the journey is over.

study.christ:
The clearest line from this chapter to Christ is drawn in John 1:14: 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us.' The verb John chooses belongs to the language of tents, and the next words, 'We have seen His glory,' recall the glory that filled the tabernacle when it was finished, Exodus 40:34. The tabernacle was God's house in the middle of Israel's camp. Jesus is God's house in the middle of humanity. The curtains of Exodus 26 hid the glory from ordinary eyes; the flesh of Jesus revealed it, 'full of grace and truth.'

The second line runs through the veil. Its purpose, verse 33, was to 'separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.' Hebrews reads this separation as a lesson: 'the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed as long as the first tabernacle was still standing,' Hebrews 9:8. When Jesus died, the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom, Matthew 27:51, and Hebrews links the curtain with His body: we enter 'by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:20. The flesh that was torn on the cross became the doorway into God's presence.

The third line runs through the high priest. Only one man could pass the veil, and only once a year. Christ has entered 'the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood,' Hebrews 9:12, and He did so as 'our forerunner,' Hebrews 6:20, which means others follow where He has gone. The difference between Exodus 26 and the gospel is not that the Most Holy Place has become less holy, but that a Priest now stands inside who has made His people fit to come in.

The fourth line is the heavenly pattern. God showed Moses a pattern, verse 30. Hebrews says Christ ministers in 'the sanctuary and true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man,' Hebrews 8:2. The earthly tent was a copy; Christ serves in the original.

There is a caution here. The New Testament does not assign meanings to the acacia frames, the silver bases or the fifty clasps. It would be easy to turn each into a picture of some aspect of Christ, but the text does not invite it. The links above are the ones Scripture itself makes, and they are rich enough. Jesus is the dwelling of God with us, the torn veil, the Priest who enters, and the minister of the true tabernacle.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who chooses to live among His people in a tent. He could have remained on the mountain or in heaven. Instead He designs a dwelling that will sit in the middle of the camp, Numbers 2:2, and move when they move. Later He reminds David, 'I have moved about with a tent as My dwelling,' 2 Samuel 7:6. God's willingness to share the conditions of a people on the road is a form of humility, and it anticipates the incarnation.

He is a God of layered holiness. The Most Holy Place is at the centre, then the Holy Place, then the courtyard, then the camp. The materials grow more precious as they come closer to Him. This is not decoration for its own sake. It is a map of what it means to approach a holy God. Leviticus 16:2 warns Aaron 'not to enter freely into the Most Holy Place behind the veil,' because God appears there.

He is also a God of beauty and order. The chapter's many measurements are not tedious to Him. He cares about loops and clasps and the fit of tenons in bases. The same God who ordered the heavens, 'He stretches out the heavens like a tent,' Psalm 104:2, orders the tent of His dwelling with the same care. The cherubim worked into the linen show that His house is meant to be glorious from the inside.

He is a God who remembers Eden. The cherubim on the veil recall those that guarded the way to the tree of life, Genesis 3:24. God has not forgotten the garden or given up on bringing His people back into His presence, but He will do it in a way that honours His holiness.

He is a God whose house rests on ransom. The silver bases were cast from the half shekel each man paid 'to atone for your lives,' Exodus 30:15 and 38:27. The dwelling of God among sinners literally stood on atonement.

And He is a God who keeps both nearness and distance in view until the day He resolves them. The veil says 'not yet'; the torn veil says 'now.'

For worship, the chapter calls believers to approach God with reverence and confidence together. Reverence, because He is holy and the veil was real. Confidence, because Hebrews says 'let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith,' Hebrews 10:22, now that Christ has opened the way.

crossReferences.note: After the fall God stations cherubim east of Eden to guard the way to the tree of life. The cherubim woven into the veil of Exodus 26:31 echo that scene. The tabernacle offers a way back toward God's presence, yet it is still a guarded way.

Every counted man pays half a shekel as a ransom for his life. According to Exodus 38:25-27 this silver was cast into the hundred bases of the sanctuary and the veil described in Exodus 26:19-32. The house of God stood on atonement money.

Assigns the Gershonites to carry the curtains and coverings and the Merarites to carry the frames, crossbars and bases. The detailed design of Exodus 26 is the design of a portable house, and these clans made it travel with the people.

Aaron is warned not to enter the Most Holy Place behind the veil at will, 'or else he will die, because I appear in the cloud above the mercy seat.' The veil of Exodus 26:33 marks a real boundary that only the Day of Atonement could cross.

When David offers to build a house of cedar, God replies that He has 'moved about with a tent as My dwelling' since the Exodus. The tabernacle of Exodus 26 was God's chosen way of living with a pilgrim people, and He had never asked for anything grander.

David longs to dwell in the house of the LORD and says God 'will conceal me under the cover of His tent.' The coverings of Exodus 26:7-14 become a picture of shelter, so that God's tent is not only a place of worship but a place of refuge.

'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us.' The verb is built on the Greek word for tent, the word the Greek Old Testament used for the tabernacle. Jesus is God pitching His tent among His people, and His glory is seen.

At Jesus' death 'the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.' The curtain Exodus 26:31-33 ordered to separate the Most Holy Place is torn by God's own hand, from above, as Christ's death opens the way.

Explains the two rooms of the tabernacle and says that the arrangement was the Holy Spirit's way of showing that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed while the first tabernacle stood. The structure of Exodus 26 is itself a lesson.

Believers have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place 'by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,' and are urged to draw near. The veil of Exodus 26 becomes a picture of Christ's flesh, and access becomes an invitation.

Paul calls the present body 'the earthly tent we live in' and longs for 'an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands.' The temporary, portable tabernacle becomes a picture of life now, awaiting a permanent dwelling with God.

'Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.' The Greek uses the language of the tabernacle. What began as a tent in the wilderness ends with God living among His people without veil or distance forever.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God walked with humanity in a garden, and after the fall cherubim barred the way back, Genesis 3:24. The question that runs through the Bible from that point is how God and sinful people can live together again. Exodus 26 gives a partial answer. God will live among them, but in a tent with layers, a veil and cherubim still standing guard.

The chapter builds on what came before. God had rescued Israel from Egypt 'so that I might dwell among them,' Exodus 29:46. He had met them on Sinai in fire and cloud. Now the mountain's presence is given a portable home. The Exodus is not complete until God lives in the camp.

It also sets up what follows. The tent travels with Israel through the wilderness, stands at Shiloh, Joshua 18:1, and then at Gibeon. It gives way to Solomon's temple, where the veil and the cherubim are repeated in stone and gold, 2 Chronicles 3:14. Yet the glory later leaves the temple, Ezekiel 10:18-19, and the prophets look for a day when God will dwell with His people in a new way, Ezekiel 37:27.

That day arrives in Jesus. The Word pitches His tent among us, John 1:14. At His death the veil is torn, and He enters the true tabernacle as the forerunner of His people, Hebrews 6:19-20. Through the Spirit the church becomes God's dwelling, Ephesians 2:22, while believers still live in bodily tents, longing for their eternal home, 2 Corinthians 5:1.

The story ends with the tent made permanent and universal. John hears the voice from the throne: 'the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them,' Revelation 21:3. The city is a perfect cube, Revelation 21:16, like the innermost room of the sanctuary, and there is no temple in it, because God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The whole new creation becomes the Most Holy Place, and no veil is needed any more.

quiz.q: What was worked into the innermost linen curtains of the tabernacle?

options.text: Cherubim, skillfully worked into blue, purple, and scarlet yarn.
options.note: Verse 1 describes the ten inner curtains this way.

options.text: Images of the twelve tribes of Israel.
options.note: The tribal names appear later on the priestly breastpiece and shoulder stones, not on these curtains.

options.text: Plain, undecorated white linen only.
options.note: The curtains were richly woven with colored yarn and cherubim, not left plain.

options.text: No decoration was included.
options.note: Verse 1 explicitly describes cherubim skillfully worked into the curtains.

quiz.q: What materials made up the outer coverings that protected the tabernacle?

options.text: Goat hair curtains, then a covering of ram skins dyed red, then fine leather.
options.note: Verses 7 and 14 describe this layered outer protection.

options.text: Solid bronze plates.
options.note: Bronze was used for bases and utensils, not as a covering layer over the tent.

options.text: A single layer of undyed wool.
options.note: The coverings were specifically goat hair, ram skins dyed red, and fine leather, not undyed wool.

options.text: No outer covering was specified.
options.note: Verses 7 through 14 explicitly describe the layered outer coverings.

quiz.q: What material and construction were the tabernacle's upright frames made of?

options.text: Acacia wood overlaid with gold, standing on silver bases.
options.note: Verses 15, 19, and 29 describe this construction.

options.text: Solid stone blocks.
options.note: The frames were wood overlaid with gold, not stone.

options.text: Bronze frames on wooden bases.
options.note: The frames themselves were acacia wood overlaid with gold, resting on silver, not bronze, bases.

options.text: The frames' material is not described.
options.note: Verses 15 through 29 explicitly describe the frames' wood, gold overlay, and silver bases.

quiz.q: What did the veil separate inside the tabernacle?

options.text: The Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.
options.note: Verse 33 states this exact function of the veil.

options.text: The courtyard from the entrance gate.
options.note: That boundary was marked by a separate gate curtain, not the inner veil described here.

options.text: The table from the lampstand.
options.note: The table and lampstand stood on opposite sides of the same Holy Place, both outside the veil.

options.text: The veil served no dividing function.
options.note: Verse 33 explicitly states the veil separates the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.

quiz.q: Where was the ark of the Testimony placed in relation to the veil?

options.text: Behind the veil, in the Most Holy Place.
options.note: Verse 33 places the ark of the Testimony behind the veil.

options.text: In front of the veil, in the Holy Place.
options.note: The table and lampstand stood in front of the veil; the ark itself was placed behind it.

options.text: Outside the tabernacle entirely.
options.note: The ark was the central furnishing kept inside, in the innermost chamber, not outside the structure.

options.text: Its placement is not specified.
options.note: Verse 33 explicitly places the ark of the Testimony behind the veil.

questions: Every layer of the tabernacle, from cherubim woven curtains to plain outer leather, moved from costly nearest God's presence to plain on the outside. Where in your own life is there a gap between how you appear outwardly and what is closest to your heart?
The veil kept even faithful Israelites from entering God's immediate presence. How often do you take for granted the access to God that Christ's torn veil has given you?

The tabernacle was God's mishkan, His dwelling place moving with His people through the wilderness. How does it change your view of God to know He chooses to dwell among His people rather than remain distant?
John says the Word tabernacled among us in Jesus. How does seeing Christ as God's true dwelling place shape the way you think about His humanity and His nearness to you?

The veil was torn at the very moment Christ died. What would it look like this week to actually live as someone with full, confident access into God's presence, rather than someone still standing outside the curtain?

translationNotes.note: Cherubim skillfully worked into the curtains recalls the cherubim guarding the way to the tree of life in Genesis 3:24, linking the tabernacle's design to the guarded holiness lost at the fall.

According to the pattern shown you on the mountain repeats language from 25:9 and 25:40, emphasizing that Moses was not designing the tabernacle himself but faithfully reproducing a pattern he was shown.

The veil, parokhet, is distinct from the outer entrance curtain in verse 36; the veil alone divides the Holy Place from the innermost Most Holy Place, and it is this veil that Matthew 27:51 records being torn at Christ's death.
